# Edit plot parts and data views

::: {.doc-lead}
Select a series, change its appearance, and adjust axes or colour scales without rerunning the analysis.
:::

## Selecting inside plots {#selecting-inside-plots}

Selection follows Figma's logic, tuned for plots:

- A **plain click** (or drag) anywhere on a plot always takes the **whole plot** — you can
  use empty space inside its rectangular bounds even when the SVG background is transparent.
  You can never accidentally drag one bar out of a chart.
- **Ctrl+click** pierces to the exact **part** under the cursor — a series' line, one point, an
  axis label — even on an unselected plot. Hold **Ctrl** and hover to preview what you'd get;
  a data part also shows its **readout** beside the box — a point's x and y, a bar's category
  and height, a hexagon's count, a heatmap cell's value, a box's statistics, a significance
  bracket's test and p — read from the plot's manifest, never from the picture.
- **Double-click** descends a level: into a group, into a plot's parts, into text editing,
  into a path's nodes.
- Whatever part you've drilled stays plain-draggable, and **Escape** steps back out one level
  at a time.

## Restyling parts {#restyling-parts}

With a part selected, press **F** to open **Properties** and restyle it — colour, width, size,
font, opacity, visibility, even a positional nudge in the plot's own units. The same fields sit in the right rail's
**Plot part** section. Part edits are stored as overrides keyed to the part's stable name, so
**they survive regeneration** of the plot. Recolouring a series' whole line or points repaints its
legend swatch too, so the key never lies about the colour; recolouring one bar or one point is a
highlight and leaves the key alone.

When the picked part belongs to a plain series, the **Plot part** section also offers **Series
colour**: one colour for the whole series — its line, its markers' faces and edges, its bars or
band, its error bars and its legend swatch — written as one override per part, so it survives
regeneration like any part edit, with **reset** to return to the generated colours. A
colour-mapped series (a heatmap, a hexbin, a scatter coloured by value) has no series colour: edit
its [**Colour scale**](#colour-scales) instead. From the command line, the same edit is
`flux set-series-color` ([command reference](/docs/commands.html#verb-cheat-sheet)).

## X-ray {#x-ray}

**Alt+R** opens the **X-ray**: the anatomy of the selected plot (or group) as a tree, placed
beside the selection.

- Walk the tree with the arrow keys, and hide or show any part with **x**.
- **Enter** (or **F**) selects the picked parts and opens their properties.
- For recipe-backed plots, **Regenerate** reruns the script that made the plot, right from
  the panel. You can inspect another plot while a recipe runs; its result still belongs to
  the plot you regenerated.
- **Double-click** a row (or press **Ctrl+Enter**) to re-root the X-ray on it. Keyboard
  navigation keeps the active row in view.

Rows **multi-select**: **Shift+click** picks a run, **Ctrl+click** toggles one, **Ctrl+A**
picks everything, **Alt+A** picks every search result, and a press-and-drag over rows picks
the run you sweep (hold **Ctrl** when you press to add a second sweep to the pick). **a**
widens the pick to its siblings: first the same part under each sibling of its parent
(*X axis › Tick marks* adds *Y axis › Tick marks*), then, pressed again, every row under the
same parent. **x**, **Enter** and the property menu then act on all of them, so you can hide
five series at once or restyle them together.

Select **several plots** before pressing **Alt+R** and the X-ray shows each plot's tree plus a
**Common parts** list of what they all share, so hiding the x-axis of four plots is one row
and one keypress.

## Dissecting a plot {#dissecting-a-plot}

A summary plot usually hides a story — twenty subjects behind one regression line, a table
of statistics behind one asterisk. **D** with a plot selected opens **Dissect**: a viewer for
that plot's *companion material*, which lives in
[`plots/_dissections/<plot name>/`](/docs/dissections.html). Drop per-subject panels,
alternative analyses, or stats CSVs there (subfolders become tabs) and they're one keypress
away from the composed figure — without ever appearing in the plot importer or your figures.

Inside the viewer: **arrow keys** move around the grid, **Enter** expands a file
(**Ctrl+scroll** zooms images at the cursor, **Space+drag** pans, **Enter** toggles fit/1:1),
CSV and TSV files open as sortable tables, and **Escape** steps back out. The **⧉** button
shrinks the viewer to a floating window you can keep beside the canvas; files dropped into
the folder while it's open appear live. The Inspector's **Dissections** button (with a count)
does the same as **D** — and for a plot with no dissections yet, it offers to create the
folder.

## Axis view {#axis-view}

Select a plot with a manifest containing series and calibrated axes to edit **Axis view** in
the Inspector. The controls are unavailable without axes and series; an unsupported axis
is disabled with its reason. Each supported axis has **min** and **max**
in data units and a **linear/log** scale. An empty field uses the generated plot's limit,
shown as its placeholder. **Reset** restores both generated axes. Typing or wheeling previews
the change; finishing the edit makes one undo step, and **Escape** cancels it.

The **F** menu offers **x view** (**v**) and **y view** (**b**); on cropped plots, follow the
row's displayed key when **v** is already assigned. Once a view is open there, the mouse wheel
adjusts the focused limit wherever the pointer is (the canvas does not zoom); **Space** accepts
the minimum and moves to the maximum, and **Space** again (or **Enter**) accepts it and returns to
the menu. In X-ray, select an axis row and press
**v** for **Axis view…** to focus that axis in the Inspector.

Lines, points, bars, heatmap cells, hexagons, contour bands and box or violin bodies re-project
inside the existing plot frame; exports include the same view. A viewed axis is re-ticked: its
generated ticks, labels and gridlines give way to a fresh set laid out for the new limits (nice
steps with matching labels on a linear axis, decades on a log one; an axis of categories, dates
or fixed labels keeps its own ticks, which move with their values and fade in the outer 4%).
Non-series marks, such as a dashed reference line, and raster layers stay put. A log view needs
positive limits and positive data. For multi-panel plots the view applies to all panels;
placeholders show the first panel.

A plot with a **twin value axis** (an `ax.twinx()` or `twiny()` in fluxplot 0.3.2 or later) shows
a **y2** (or **x2**) row too: the twin's own limits and scale, applied to the series drawn on it
while the panel's other series stay where they are. A secondary axis that only relabels its
parent through a function follows the parent and has no row of its own.

## Colour scales {#colour-scales}

A colour-mapped plot saved by fluxplot 0.3.1 or later (hexbin, heatmap, scatter with `c=`,
contour bands, colour-mapped bars and lines) records each colour scale's exact law — its colormap
table, its normalisation and limits — and every coloured element's data value. Select the plot to
edit **Colour scales** in the Inspector, one block per scale.

In the **F** menu, the **colour scale** row (**c**, or the key the row displays) opens the
editor with the whole menu to itself, widened to fit: the controls on the left and the palette
list always open on the right, so trying a palette is one click (or **↑/↓** and **Enter**);
**Escape** returns to the other properties. X-ray shows the same controls under the plot's
regenerate controls; it widens while its palette list is open, and a wide list shows each
type's maps in two columns.

- **Palette** takes any colormap fluxplot ships, typed by name or picked from the collections
  behind the preview bar. **Reverse** flips it.
- **Norm** offers the kinds the scale allows (linear, log, power, symlog). A centre appears
  for two-slope norms, gamma for power, and the linear threshold and scale for symlog.
- **Min** and **max** are in data units. **Extend** chooses which out-of-range arrows the key
  shows.

Every element recolours as you type, together with the key's gradient and its ticks, and
nothing regenerates. An empty field uses the generated value shown as its placeholder;
finishing an edit makes one undo step, **Escape** cancels it and **Reset** restores the
generated scale. An edit that cannot be painted, such as a log minimum at zero or a minimum
above the maximum, is refused with its reason and the plot keeps the last valid colours. A
scale that also carries an **opacity channel** (fluxplot's `alpha_by`: a hexagon's count, a
cell's p-value) keeps every element's opacity through a recolour; the block names the channel
and its range, and the channel itself is edited in the source.

Live edits are element state: they are saved with the figure, honoured by exports and Paper
embeds, tween in slides and travel with copies of the plot. **Apply to source** writes the
complete colour controls of every scale into the plot's recipe, regenerates the plot from its
data and clears the live edit, so the source file paints the same colours; it needs a runnable
recipe. A scale drawn as one raster image reports itself and can only regenerate. Older plots
without a recorded scale keep the regenerate-only palette and range fields.

From the command line, the same edit is `flux set-plot-color-scale`. On slides, a colour-scale
change can also animate between steps; see
[Transforms and data morphs](/docs/transforms.html#colour-scale-recolouring-in-data-units).

## View as {#view-as}

**View as…** in the toolbar shows the whole canvas the way a colour-deficient reader sees it —
**deuteranopia**, **protanopia**, **tritanopia** (Machado 2009 at full severity, the same
simulation fluxplot's accessibility lint uses) — or in **greyscale** (luminance, what a
black-and-white print keeps). It is a way of looking, applied as a display filter over the canvas: nothing
in the figure changes, exports are untouched, and it lasts for the session. Use it while choosing
series colours or a colormap; a pair of series that merge under deuteranopia need a different pair.
